source.title: Probing the Knowledge Boundary: An Interactive Agentic Framework for Deep Knowledge Extraction
source.authors: Yu-Heng Yang; Si-Qi Zhu; Tao Feng; Ge Liu; Jia-Xuan You

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. No truncation or garbling noted.
record.tranche_reason: The paper presents its knowledge-volume scaling analysis as an extension of prior loss/perplexity scaling work, but measures extracted knowledge coverage rather than the loss behaviors in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. and says its scaling analysis extends prior work from loss/perplexity to knowledge volume. Its own scale results measure knowledge-union recall and audit accuracy, not held-out pretraining loss, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. These results are recorded under fits_no_version. Strategy-comparison and fine-tuning results do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper presents its 'knowledge scaling law' as extending Kaplan and Hoffmann from loss to knowledge volume, but it measures no pretraining loss, fits no power law, makes no extrapolation and runs no compute-allocation or shape sweep. The closest version is V6 (downstream predictability). The only scale result is a three-point comparison of Llama-3.1 Instruct models (8B/70B/405B). Its metric is recall relative to a pooled union of only the compared models' outputs, under a pipeline the authors call 'operational and pipeline-dependent'. No prediction from scale or loss is made or checked. So this is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version, not a test of V6. T6 is used because the study neither tests nor relies on the loss-scaling finding as a tool; it only discusses it.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that extractable knowledge grows with model size (recall 27.3% at 8B to 39.0% at 405B), call this a 'Knowledge Scaling Law', and note diminishing returns plus a slight accuracy regression at 405B. They also conclude that Recursive Taxonomy is the best probing strategy, that RL code specialization narrows recall and harms out-of-domain accuracy, and that training-data composition shapes each model family's knowledge profile.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses an interactive taxonomy-based extraction pipeline and measures knowledge-union recall and audit accuracy, rather than measuring held-out cross-entropy loss or fitting loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Knowledge-extraction estimates vary with deduplication thresholds and prompt wording: across the stated threshold sweep, recall varied by at most ±0.017 and accuracy by at most ±0.005, while model ordering was preserved; synonym substitutions changed raw atom count by +6.3%.

fits_no_version.finding: Under TAXONOMY-L5W5, average union-relative recall rises 27.3% (8B), 36.9% (70B), 39.0% (405B). Gains diminish (+9.6 pp vs +2.1 pp). Audit accuracy is non-monotonic: 81.2%, 89.0%, 87.7%. The 405B>70B>8B recall ordering is preserved across a 9-setting deduplication-threshold sweep.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within the Llama-3.1 Instruct family, larger models yield more extractable valid domain knowledge under a fixed agentic probing pipeline, with diminishing recall gains at the largest size.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix Table 4 gives absolute valid-atom counts per size. For example, Deep Learning: 2454 (8B), 3746 (70B), 3589 (405B); ML Systems: 2873, 4111, 4757. The 405B model does not always yield more valid atoms than 70B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Absolute extractable knowledge counts do not rise monotonically with size in every domain, even when union-relative recall does.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The measured outcome is pipeline-dependent knowledge coverage rather than loss. Scaling is compared at only three model sizes, with no power-law fit or extrapolation test. The paper reports conflicting per-domain values for the same scaling results in Table 1 and Appendix Table 6, although their reported averages agree. No uncertainty estimate is stated for the scaling averages.
record.rows_left_out: Per-domain scaling values were not entered as separate rows because Table 1 and Appendix Table 6 report conflicting per-domain figures for the same models; the shared three-domain averages are recorded instead.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No depth/width or architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime examined for power-law loss.
No standard downstream task scores and no predictive relation to scale or loss. Recall is relative to a pooled union of the compared models and is measured at three sizes without a fit.
The threshold and prompt sensitivity checks concern extraction metrics, not fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits.

missing.what: Absolute raw, unique and valid atom counts per model size and domain, which show 405B below 70B in valid atoms for Deep Learning. Relevant only to the fits_no_version finding.

record.verdict_notes: This is a borderline call for V6. A capability rising with size could be read as downstream scaling. It was excluded for three reasons: the metric is relative to a pool built from the compared models themselves, only three post-trained checkpoints are compared, and no predictive or power-law relation is tested. The record correctly flags that the per-domain values in Table 1 and Appendix Table 6 disagree, while the averages match. All rows correctly carry versions ['none'] with state cannot_determine, so no row fixes are needed. The reader's tranche T3 was changed to T6, because T3 denotes a test in a new setting, which this study is not.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute is not measured.
The study does not fit loss curves on smaller runs or test predictions on larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split is tested.
The study does not vary depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count to measure loss.
No other modality or training regime is tested for the claimed loss power-law form.
The study does not test downstream-task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity tests concern knowledge-extraction recall and accuracy, not fitted loss exponents, loss-curve bending, or compute-optimal allocation.
